title_en: Ma Shengzhong v. The People's Government of Guyuan City, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region and Guyuan City Housing and Urban-Rural Construction Bureau, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region — dispute over administrative approval and housing demolition administrative ruling
ruling_gist_en: In an administrative case, the challenged administrative act generally refers to only one administrative act made by one administrative agency, or the same administrative act made by two or more administrative agencies. In the absence of legal provisions, unless there are special circumstances such as related facts and out of consideration for judicial economy and convenience, two or more administrative acts generally shall not be listed as challenged administrative acts in the same administrative case.
keywords_en: administrative; administrative reply; administrative adjudication on house demolition; second instance; Supreme People's Court; Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region; natural person; state organ; Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China; Regulations on the Administration of Urban House Demolition; limitation period for filing a lawsuit; joint lawsuit of multiple challenged administrative acts; dismissal of claims; house demolition; administrative adjudication
full_text_en:
Ma Shengzhong v. People's Government of Guyuan City, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region (administrative approval) and Housing and Urban-Rural Construction Bureau of Guyuan City, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region (administrative ruling on house demolition)

Ruling Summary

In an administrative case, the alleged administrative act generally refers only to a single administrative act made by one administrative agency, or the same administrative act made by two or more administrative agencies. Unless otherwise provided by law, and except under special circumstances such as related facts or for the sake of procedural economy, generally two or more administrative acts shall not be listed as the alleged administrative acts in the same administrative case.

Supreme People's Court Administrative Ruling

(2019) Supreme People's Court Administrative Final No. 1

Appellant (plaintiff at first instance): Ma Shengzhong, male, born on April 11, 1954, Hui ethnicity, residing in Xingqing District, Yinchuan City, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region.

Appellant Ma Shengzhong, in the case concerning his lawsuit against the People's Government of Guyuan City, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region (hereinafter referred to as Guyuan City Government) regarding an administrative approval and against the Housing and Urban-Rural Construction Bureau of Guyuan City, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region (hereinafter referred to as the Housing Bureau) regarding an administrative ruling on house demolition, appealed against the administrative ruling (2019) Ning Xing Chu No. 1 rendered by the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region High People's Court on January 15, 2019, and filed an appeal with this Court. This Court lawfully formed a collegial panel and heard the case. The trial is now concluded.

The court of first instance received on October 12, 2018, a statement of complaint filed by Ma Shengzhong naming the Guyuan City Government as the defendant. After being given clarification by that court, Ma Shengzhong amended the statement of complaint on January 14, 2019, adding the former Guyuan City Construction Bureau (now renamed the Housing and Urban-Rural Construction Bureau of Guyuan City) as a defendant. Ma Shengzhong alleged in the complaint that: (1) the administrative approval act in the Reply on the Base Price for Compensation for House Demolition and Standards for Temporary Relocation Subsidies (Gu Zheng Han (2003) No. 3, hereinafter referred to as Reply No. 3) issued by the Guyuan City Government on March 18, 2003, concerning the "replacement price for house demolition", violated Article 24 of the State Council's Regulations on the Administration of Urban House Demolition and Article 27 of the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region Measures for the Administration of Urban House Demolition, infringed upon the lawful rights and interests of the demolished party in the house demolition appraisal, and should be found to be illegal; (2) the defendant was the house expropriation department for Guyuan City in 2003 and 2006, and had the authority to formulate measures for the demolition, relocation, and compensation of houses in the city, but in this case exercised its power to determine the city's "replacement price for house demolition" through Reply No. 3 and the Notice on Standardizing Compensation for House Demolition (Gu Zheng Fa (2006) No. 83, hereinafter referred to as Notice No. 83), thereby stopping the implementation of the house demolition compensation method stipulated in the Interim Measures for the Administration of Urban House Demolition in Guyuan City, which had been discussed and passed by the standing committee of the people's government at that level and promulgated as Government Order No. 5, infringing upon the lawful rights and interests of the demolished party. He requested that the defendant Guyuan City Government provide compensation for the compensation for the demolished house itself, temporary relocation subsidy expenses, and losses caused by the cessation of business due to the demolition, all of which were supported by sufficient evidence. Therefore, he requested: (1) a judgment confirming that the administrative act of the Guyuan City Government in replying on March 18, 2003, to the city's "replacement price for house demolition" was illegal; (2) a judgment revoking the specific act of the former Guyuan City Construction Bureau in its House Demolition Ruling No. (2006) 02 (hereinafter referred to as Demolition Ruling No. 02); (3) a judgment confirming that the administrative act of the Guyuan City Government on June 15, 2006, in stopping the implementation of part of the content of the people's government's Order No. 5 was illegal; (4) a concurrent review of the normative documents, namely Notice No. 83 and Gu Zheng Fa (2007) No. 87 (hereinafter referred to as Notice No. 87); (5) a concurrent resolution of the issue of providing the demolished party (the plaintiff) with housing for living; (6) a judgment ordering the defendants to compensate for losses totaling RMB 3,082,631.25 arising from the two demolitions of his house built on state-owned land with a total floor area of 422.69 square meters, for which compensation had not been paid in accordance with the regulations; and (7) all litigation costs of this case to be borne by the defendants.

The court of first instance held that a party filing an administrative lawsuit with a people's court should assert its rights within the statutory time limit. The facts concerning the demolition and resettlement of the relevant property of the plaintiff Ma Shengzhong, as well as the relevant administrative acts of the Guyuan City Government and the former Guyuan City Construction Bureau, all occurred before 2008. During the demolition and resettlement of the property involved, there existed both a house demolition ruling made by the former Guyuan City Construction Bureau and a demolition (resettlement) agreement signed between Ma Shengzhong and the Guyuan City Municipal Company, and Ma Shengzhong had already received the corresponding demolition and resettlement compensation, so there was no scenario where Ma Shengzhong was unaware of the content of the relevant administrative acts. Article 41 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "When an administrative agency makes a specific administrative act without informing a citizen, legal person, or other organization of the right to sue or the time limit for filing a lawsuit, the time limit for filing a lawsuit shall be calculated from the date on which the citizen, legal person, or other organization knows or should know the right to sue or the time limit for filing a lawsuit, but the maximum shall not exceed two years from the date on which it knows or should know the content of the specific administrative act." The plaintiff Ma Shengzhong filed a lawsuit with the people's court on October 12, 2018, which had already exceeded the statutory time limit for filing a lawsuit and without legitimate reasons. Pursuant to Article 51, Paragraph 2 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court ruled not to accept the case filed by Ma Shengzhong.

Ma Shengzhong appealed, arguing that his lawsuit met the conditions for filing under Article 52 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and the court of first instance erred in refusing to accept the case. (1) The alleged acts in this case were administrative acts made by the Guyuan City Government in connection with the expropriation of houses, and the expropriated houses were immovable property. For cases involving immovable property, if a lawsuit is filed more than twenty years after the date of the administrative act, the people's court shall not accept it. The initial administrative act in this case occurred on March 18, 2003, followed by June 15, 2006. He filed the lawsuit asserting his rights on October 12, 2018, which was within the time limit. (2) The court of first instance accepted the administrative complaint on October 12, 2018, only after the People's Procuratorate of the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region exercised legal supervision over the acceptance of the complaint, but did not issue a written receipt. Before sending the ruling, it did not issue a notice of acceptance of the administrative case, nor did it inform him of the composition of the collegial panel. The case processing procedures of the court of first instance violated Article 51 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. (3) The court of first instance neither accepted the case nor held a hearing, and sua sponte applied the statute of limitations provisions, which violated Article 193 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China. Therefore, he requested this Court to set aside the ruling of the court of first instance and order the court of first instance to accept the case in accordance with the law.

After examining the evidence materials submitted by the appellant Ma Shengzhong when filing this lawsuit, this Court finds the following relevant circumstances concerning Reply No. 3, Demolition Ruling No. 02, Notice No. 83, and Notice No. 87, which are the subject of his claims: (1) Reply No. 3 was made by the Guyuan City Government on March 18, 2003, in response to the Request for Instructions on Submitting the Base Price for Compensation for House Demolition and Standards for Temporary Relocation Subsidies in Guyuan City submitted by the former Guyuan City Construction Bureau. The main content of the reply was: "1. Replacement price (base price) for house demolition: brick-concrete multi-story buildings: RMB 500 per square meter... 2. Temporary relocation subsidy: residential use: RMB 3 per square meter per month... 3. Relocation subsidy: RMB 3 per square meter." (2) Demolition Ruling No. 02 was made by the former Guyuan City Construction Bureau on September 1, 2006. The ruling stated that the applicant was the "Guyuan City Municipal Company" and the respondent was "Ma Shengzhong." It also stated: "If the parties are not satisfied with this ruling, they may apply for administrative reconsideration within 60 days from receipt of this ruling or file a lawsuit with the people's court within 3 months from receipt of this ruling." (3) Notice No. 83 was made by the Guyuan City Government on June 15, 2006, to "all county (district) people's governments, all departments and directly affiliated institutions of the municipal government, and all enterprises and institutions." The relevant modifications and adjustments to Guyuan City Government Order No. 5 in this notice were: "Implement Article 18 of the Interim Measures for the Administration of Urban House Demolition in Guyuan City, as promulgated by Guyuan City Government Order No. 5, and adjust it to 'The method of compensation for demolition and resettlement shall only be the exchange of property rights (exchange of equivalent value)'; cease implementation of Article 19... and adjust it to 'Appraisal shall be conducted by a qualified house appraisal intermediary institution on the basis of replacement price'; cease implementation of Article 21..." (4) Notice No. 87 was titled "Notice on Ceasing Implementation of the Notice on Standardizing Compensation for House Demolition of Guyuan City Government." This notice was made by the Guyuan City Government on July 27, 2007, to "all county (district) people's governments, and relevant directly affiliated units of the municipal government." The main content was: "1. Cease implementation of the Notice on Standardizing Compensation for House Demolition of Guyuan City Government (Gu Zheng Fa (2006) No. 83). 2. The original compensation standards for attachments on collectively owned land expropriated within the Guyuan city planning area shall remain unchanged and shall be separately announced. 3. This notice shall take effect from the date of issuance."

This Court holds that regarding the lawsuit filed by the appellant Ma Shengzhong, the court of first instance ruled not to accept the case based on Article 51, Paragraph 2 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. The core dispute in this case is whether the appellant's lawsuit meets the statutory conditions for filing. Article 49, Item 3 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, which requires "a specific claim," is one of the statutory conditions for filing. It is generally understood that "a specific claim" mainly refers to a specific and definite alleged administrative act. The alleged administrative act constitutes the object of the people's court's legality review and also determines the scope of the court's trial and judgment. In an administrative case, the alleged administrative act generally refers only to a single administrative act made by one administrative agency, or the same administrative act made by two or more administrative agencies. Although a citizen, legal person, or other organization may raise multiple claims that are logically interconnected when filing a lawsuit, the alleged administrative act serving as the basis for the claims must be one. This is the principle of "one act, one lawsuit" in the acceptance of administrative cases, commonly referred to as such. Different administrative acts have different subjects, the substantive and procedural laws on which they are based differ, the facts on which they rest are different, and the scope, content, and intensity of the people's court's legality review are not entirely the same. If two or more administrative acts are challenged in the same administrative case, it would not only hinder the effective response of the administrative agencies but also inevitably impede the orderly conduct of litigation activities by the people's court, such as focusing on the alleged administrative act, summarizing the points of dispute, organizing the presentation and cross-examination of evidence, determining the facts of the case, arranging court arguments, accurately applying the law, and making clear and definite judgments. This would in turn affect the fair and timely adjudication of the administrative case, the protection of the lawful rights and interests of citizens, legal persons, and other organizations, and the exercise of the judicial function of supervising administrative agencies in exercising their powers according to law. It also would not contribute to the targeted promotion of the substantive resolution of administrative disputes. This principle is inherent in the rules of administrative litigation. Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, concerning the joint defendants of administrative agencies that jointly make the same administrative act, and Article 27, concerning necessary joint actions arising from the same administrative act, typically reflect this principle. Unless otherwise provided by law, and except under special circumstances such as related facts or for the sake of procedural economy, generally two or more administrative acts shall not be listed as the alleged administrative acts in the same administrative case. Article 26, Paragraph 2 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, concerning joint defendants when the reexamination agency upholds the original administrative act, is a very exceptional procedural arrangement in administrative litigation. Even so, pursuant to Article 135, Paragraph 1 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on the Application of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the legality of the original administrative act remains the focus of the review, and the legality of the reconsideration decision is only reviewed concurrently. It should also be noted that Article 27 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, concerning ordinary joint actions arising from similar administrative acts, provides for the joinder of two or more independent administrative cases for trial, not for a single administrative case. In this case, the appellant's first six claims challenged multiple acts, which clearly violated this principle and rendered the claims not specific. However, pursuant to Article 68, Paragraph 3 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on the Application of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the people's court should provide necessary guidance and clarification to assist citizens, legal persons, or other organizations with insufficient litigation capacity in properly identifying a single alleged administrative act in one administrative case. The ruling of the court of first instance does not show that the court provided such guidance and clarification, which was somewhat inappropriate. However, from the subsequent analysis of each of the appellant's claims, it can be seen that this inappropriateness did not affect the lawful and reasonable exercise of the appellant's right to sue.

The first and third claims challenged Reply No. 3 and Notice No. 83. From this Court's examination, Reply No. 3 and Notice No. 83 were internal replies made by the Guyuan City Government to relevant units. They did not directly produce legal effects on the rights and obligations of specific citizens, legal persons, or other organizations and are not actionable administrative acts.

The second claim involved Demolition Ruling No. 02 made by the former Guyuan City Construction Bureau. From this Court's examination, when the former Guyuan City Construction Bureau made this demolition ruling on September 1, 2006, it informed the appellant of the right to sue and the time limit for filing a lawsuit. The appellant's challenge to this demolition ruling far exceeded the three-month time limit for filing a lawsuit under Article 39 of the then-effective Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (prior to amendment), and the evidence materials he submitted did not show any legitimate reason for exceeding the statutory time limit for filing a lawsuit. Since the appellant was already aware of the content of this demolition ruling, his argument for applying the twenty-year maximum limitation period for protection is untenable. The statute of limitations is a provision of substantive civil law, while the time limit for filing a lawsuit is a provision of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. Filing a lawsuit within the statutory time limit is one of the statutory conditions for filing, and the people's court should examine it ex officio. The ruling of the court of first instance was based on the finding that the appellant's lawsuit in this case exceeded the statutory time limit for filing without legitimate reason, not on the application of the statute of limitations as the appellant claimed. Therefore, the appellant's argument that the court of first instance violated Article 193 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China is also unfounded.

The fourth claim involved Article 53, Paragraph 1 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, concerning the incidental review of normative documents in administrative litigation. However, one of the preconditions for such incidental review is that the lawsuit challenging the administrative act meets the statutory conditions for filing. If the lawsuit challenging the administrative act is not established, the incidental review of the normative document has no basis. This is the case with the appellant's request to review Notice No. 83 and Notice No. 87. Moreover, the appellant simultaneously challenged Notice No. 83 and requested a review of it as a normative document, which clearly violates the law.

Regarding the fifth claim, the evidence materials submitted by the appellant, including Demolition Ruling No. 02 and the demolition agreement, show that he was the demolished party, and the party obligated to provide compensation and resettlement was the demolishing party, the Guyuan City Municipal Company. Neither the Guyuan City Government nor the former Guyuan City Construction Bureau was the demolishing party, nor was there any scenario, as the appellant claimed on appeal, where the Guyuan City Government made an administrative act in connection with the expropriation of the house. Furthermore, the appellant did not deny in his appeal the finding of the court of first instance that he had already received the corresponding demolition and resettlement compensation. Therefore, the appellant's request for a concurrent resolution of the issue of providing him with housing for living clearly lacks factual basis.

The sixth claim was for administrative compensation. Pursuant to Article 4 of the State Compensation Law of the People's Republic of China, the existence of an illegal administrative act is a basic prerequisite for a citizen, legal person, or other organization to obtain administrative compensation for damage to property rights. The appellant requested compensation for the losses caused by the two demolitions of his house on state-owned land, but he did not submit evidence proving that the Guyuan City Government or the former Guyuan City Construction Bureau had carried out the act of demolishing his house. The evidence materials he submitted also cannot establish the possibility that these two agencies demolished his house or that they should bear legal liability for the demolition carried out by other entities. Therefore, this claim clearly lacks a basis.

Thus, even when each of the appellant's six claims is examined individually, they do not meet the statutory conditions for filing a lawsuit.

The appellant also claimed that the court of first instance violated Article 51 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. The court of first instance reviewed the complaint submitted by the appellant and rendered a ruling not to accept the case. Considering the above analysis of the appellant's claims, even if the appellant's statement were true, any irregularities that should be corrected did not have a material impact on the lawful and reasonable exercise of the appellant's right to sue, nor can it prove that his lawsuit in this case met the statutory conditions for filing.

In conclusion, the lawsuit filed by the appellant Ma Shengzhong does not meet the statutory conditions for filing, and this Court does not support his appeal. The court of first instance's ruling to reject the appellant's lawsuit on the general ground that it exceeded the statutory time limit for filing had flaws in fact-finding and application of law, but the result was correct and should be affirmed. Pursuant to Article 89, Paragraph 1, Item 1 and Article 101 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 334 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, this Court rules as follows:

Appeal dismissed and the original ruling affirmed.
This ruling is final.
